name: Battle of Guandu
info: In 200 CE, late in the Eastern Han dynasty, the warlord Cao Cao held the fortified camp at Guandu against the larger army of Yuan Shao, burned Yuan's grain at Wuchao and routed him, becoming the dominant power in northern China.

facts.date: 200 CE; the siege of Guandu ran from the eighth to the tenth month
facts.place: Guandu, north-east of present-day Zhongmu County, Henan, China, near the Yellow River and on the road to the capital Xu; the supply depot at Wuchao lay 40 li away
facts.sides: Cao Cao, with Emperor Xian in his capital Xu, against Yuan Shao, whose army is said to have numbered up to 110,000, including 10,000 cavalry; Xun Yu's letter to Cao Cao has him holding with one-tenth of the enemy's force
facts.outcome: Cao Cao burned almost all of Yuan Shao's food at Wuchao and destroyed his army; Yuan Shao fled north across the Yellow River with only about 800 cavalry.

t: Yuan Shao's army was larger, said to number up to 110,000 men, but Cao Cao's small cavalry raids on his supply depots at Gushi and then Wuchao decided the campaign.
Yuan Shao ignored the advice of Ju Shou, Tian Feng and Xu You at several points, and Xu You then defected and told Cao Cao where Wuchao was weakly guarded.
Yuan Shao died in June 202 and his sons fought each other, so that by 207 most of northern China was under Cao Cao.
dyk: In his proclamation of victory to Emperor Xian, Cao Cao claimed to have killed 70,000 enemy troops.
ev: Cao Cao defeats Lü Bu at Xiapi and in the autumn stations troops at Guandu and prepares fortifications
Liu Bei rebels and seizes Xu Province, and Cao Cao turns east and retakes it
Yuan Shao marches to Liyang, and Yan Liang and Wen Chou are killed in the first skirmishes
Yuan Shao advances from Yangwu in the eighth month and the armies settle into trench warfare at Guandu
In the ninth month Cao Cao's cavalry burns Yuan Shao's grain carts at Gushi
In the tenth month Cao Cao raids Wuchao by night, Zhang He and Gao Lan surrender, and Yuan Shao's army collapses
Yuan Shao dies in June and his sons Yuan Tan and Yuan Shang begin to fight each other
Yuan Shang and Yuan Xi are killed by Gongsun Kang, who sends their heads to Cao Cao

sections.background:
By 196 a clash between Cao Cao and Yuan Shao had become apparent. Yuan Shao held the lands north of the Yellow River, the Hebei region. Cao Cao controlled most of the lands south of it after defeating Lü Bu at the Battle of Xiapi in 199, and kept Emperor Xian with him in the new capital city of Xu. Each saw the other as the obvious obstacle to his own ambition to conquer and rule China. Tension grew after Cao Cao moved Emperor Xian from the old capital Luoyang.

Some years before the battle Yuan Shao's advisors Ju Shou and Tian Feng warned that Cao Cao would become a threat and advised him to attack while Cao Cao was still building up his forces. Yuan Shao ignored them, as Cao Cao was still nominally an ally. In the first month of 200 Liu Bei rebelled against Cao Cao and seized Xu Province after killing Che Zhou, Cao Cao's appointed Inspector. Cao Cao left his northern front exposed and turned east to retake the province. Yuan Shao tried to use the chance to campaign south but was daunted by Yu Jin, the defender of Yan Ford.

When Cao Cao returned to Guandu after beating Liu Bei, who then sought refuge under Yuan Shao, Yuan Shao decided to renew the campaign. Tian Feng advised against it, reasoning that the chance had been lost, and was imprisoned on a charge of demoralising the army. Yuan Shao then had Chen Lin draft a document condemning Cao Cao, in effect a declaration of war, and marched his main army to the forward base of Liyang north of the river.
sections.forces:
Guandu, north-east of present-day Zhongmu County in Henan, was strategically vital. It stood near Yan Ford on the Yellow River and on the road to the capital Xu. Cao Cao saw its importance and in the autumn of 199 stationed troops there and prepared fortifications. Other posts along the frontline were held by Liu Yan at Boma, Yu Jin at Yan Ford, Cheng Yu at Juancheng and Xiahou Dun at Meng Ford. Cao Cao also sent Zang Ba to harass Qing Province, governed by Yuan Shao's son Yuan Tan, to protect his eastern flank.

Yuan Shao's army at Liyang boasted numbers of up to 110,000, including 10,000 cavalry. Despite his early successes Cao Cao was still outnumbered. In a letter Xun Yu, who defended the capital Xu, wrote that with one-tenth of the enemy's force Cao Cao had held the ground he had marked for half a year. When Cao Cao later raided Wuchao he took 5,000 infantry and cavalry, leaving Cao Hong and Xun You in charge of the main camp.

Cao Cao's advisors included Xun You, Xun Yu and Jia Xu, and his commanders Yu Jin, Xu Huang, Zhang Liao, Yue Jin and Cao Ren. Yuan Shao's advisors Ju Shou, Tian Feng, Xu You and Guo Tu disagreed with one another and with him, and his generals included Yan Liang, Wen Chou, Chunyu Qiong, Zhang He and Gao Lan. After the early skirmishes Cao Cao gave up the forward bases along the river to make a determined defence at Guandu.
sections.course:
Yuan Shao's general Yan Liang crossed the Yellow River and besieged Cao Cao's fort at Boma. On Xun You's advice Cao Cao feinted towards Yan Ford, and Yuan Shao split his troops to meet it, leaving Yan Liang unsupported. Cao Cao struck east to lift the siege, and Yan Liang was killed by Guan Yu. As Cao Cao evacuated Boma, Wen Chou and Liu Bei pursued with 6,000 horsemen. Cao Cao had his men discard horses, weapons and valuables along the road; Yuan Shao's troops broke ranks to pick them up, and 600 elite cavalry under Zhang Liao and Xu Huang ambushed them. Wen Chou was killed and Liu Bei fled.

Yuan Shao's army pushed to Yangwu, north of Guandu, and in the eighth month advanced south; the two sides fought a trench war behind earthen embankments. Yuan Shao built siege-ramps and high platforms for archers, and Cao Cao's men answered with traction trebuchets that destroyed them. Yuan Shao tried to tunnel under the fort, and Cao Cao had a large ditch dug inside his lines to block the tunnels. Neither side could overcome the other. As Cao Cao's supplies ran short, Xun Yu urged him in a letter not to retreat.

In the ninth month Xu Huang and Shi Huan led small cavalry units against the depot at Gushi, routed Han Meng and burned Yuan Shao's grain carts. In the tenth month the defector Xu You told Cao Cao that Wuchao was weakly guarded. Cao Cao attacked it by night, disguised as a reinforcement, while Yuan Shao sent Zhang He and Gao Lan against Guandu and only a small cavalry unit to Wuchao. Almost all the grain was burned. Zhang He and Gao Lan surrendered to Cao Hong, and Cao Cao attacked in full.
sections.aftermath:
The raid on Wuchao inflicted over a thousand casualties. Yuan Shao's officers Lü Weihuang, Han Juzi, Sui Yuanjin and Zhao Rui were beheaded, and Chunyu Qiong was captured by Yue Jin and had his nose cut off. Almost all of Yuan Shao's food at Wuchao was burnt. Cao Cao also cut off the noses of the dead, mixed them with the noses and lips of oxen and horses, and showed them to Yuan Shao's men as intimidation. At Guandu Yuan Shao's numerous armies were destroyed and much of his supplies were captured. Yuan Shao fled north across the Yellow River with only about 800 cavalry, and order was restored only when he reached the camp of Jiang Yiqu.

Some of Yuan Shao's men could not cross the river in time and were captured, Ju Shou among them. Some had feigned surrender in order to escape later, and Cao Cao had these men buried alive. In his proclamation of victory to Emperor Xian he claimed to have killed 70,000 enemy troops.

Yuan Shao died in June 202 and his youngest son Yuan Shang succeeded him. The eldest, Yuan Tan, was furious and fought his brother, and the advisors and generals divided into two factions. Cao Cao attacked Yuan Tan's base at Liyang and withdrew, but the brothers went to open war. Yuan Tan allied with Cao Cao, who accused him of violating the terms and killed him in battle. Yuan Shang fled north to Yuan Xi, and after the Battle of White Wolf Mountain they took refuge in Liaodong in 207 with Gongsun Kang, who killed them and sent their heads to Cao Cao.
sections.sources:
The one figure for the enemy dead is Cao Cao's own claim, in his proclamation of victory to Emperor Xian, to have killed 70,000 troops, a claim made by the winner. The strength of Yuan Shao's army, up to 110,000 with 10,000 cavalry, is its own boast.

Dispute lies mostly in how the battle has been read. The Song dynasty historian Sima Guang, compiler of the Zizhi Tongjian, held that Yuan Shao was generous, elegant and able, but obstinate, self-satisfied and seldom heeded reasonable advice, and that these faults caused his defeat. The Chinese Nationalists followed traditional historiography in judging the battle by personalities rather than by situations and tactics. The historian Carl Leban credits Cao Cao's victory to one strategic decision, the choice of Guandu as the place to stand, which stretched Yuan Shao's supply lines.

The Australian sinologist Rafe de Crespigny is sceptical of the traditional view and questions Yuan Shao's supposed advantage. He argues that Yuan Shao's hold on his territories was less secure than Cao Cao's, and notes that Yuan Shao took ten years to eliminate the isolated Gongsun Zan. On this view he may not have had the men to spare for the ventures he is blamed for neglecting, and his decisions may not have been as foolish as traditional historians have said.
sections.legacy:
The battle was the point at which Cao Cao became the dominant power in northern China, which led to the establishment of the state of Cao Wei in the Three Kingdoms period. By 207 most of northern China was unified under his control, and he could turn his attention to the south. The victory is called decisive, the turning point of the war between the two warlords and the climactic event of Cao Cao's life.

Later commentators and military writers have studied it hoping to imitate his success. In the twentieth century the Chinese Nationalists and Communists each made their own interpretation. Mao Zedong, writing on strategic retreat, set Guandu beside the battles of Chenggao, Kunyang, Red Cliffs, Xiaoting and the Fei River. In all of them, he wrote, the contestants were unequal in strength, and the weaker one, yielding a step at first, pinned down the stronger through delayed action and defeated him.

Mao's words drew attention to the battle, and many papers analysed it in Maoist terms. That reading notes Yuan Shao's serious errors of judgement and holds that a strong enemy will make fateful errors which the weaker opponent need only wait for. The Marxist interpretation portrays Yuan Shao as the representative of the great landlord-official class and Cao Cao as of the middle and small landlord class, so that the battle was a product of class conflict and Yuan Shao's fall inevitable.

summary: In 200 CE Cao Cao held the camp at Guandu against Yuan Shao's larger army, burned its grain at Wuchao and broke it. Yuan Shao fled north with about 800 cavalry, and Cao Cao went on to control most of northern China.
notes: Cao Cao's strength is not given; only Xun Yu's letter (one-tenth of the enemy's force) and the 5,000 of the Wuchao raid. The article's 'still outnumbered' is used.
The article names no primary sources for the battle, so the sources section turns to the commentators and the disputes; it is short.
Wen Chou's pursuit: the article says Wen Chou and Liu Bei led 6,000 horsemen; Liu Bei is elsewhere said to have rebelled and sought refuge with Yuan Shao.
The article calls the victory 'decisive' and Cao Cao 'impressive'; I kept 'decisive' with its reason.
Left out: Chen Lin's document text, Cao Ren's actions against Liu Pi and Han Meng, Yuan Shao's rejected plans from Ju Shou and Xu You in detail, Gong Du's raids, Sima Guang's sentence on Cao Cao.
The article says Xun Yu defended Xu and also that Cao Cao 'abandoned the forward bases'; both kept as written.
